title: AI Agents: Model vs. Agentic Harness
transcript: You might have noticed that two AI products can feel completely different even when they're running the same underlying model, like how the same model could be a basic back and forth chatbot, but if you put it inside a developer tool with access to files and a terminal, it can suddenly work for hours on a software task. So what accounts for the difference? Well it comes down to AI model and a gentic harness. And let's start with AI model, because what that is is pretty simple. We all know what these AI models are, things like chatGPT or maybe Claude. So when we talk about a model, we really mean the actual artificial neural network. And what those models can't really do on their own is reach out into the world. They can't open a file or run a piece of code natively. They can't really browse the web either. So on their own, these AI models are essentially a brain in a jar. They're capable, but they're trapped in that jar. Now a benchmark gaps between the top labs have narrowed to within a few points of each other on most e-vails. So when one AI product clearly outperforms another, the brain itself, which I mean the AI model, that usually isn't the explanation. It spots rapid around the brain. And that wrapping has a name. When we take a model and we wrap it, we are calling this thing that wraps it the agentic harness. And then if we think of an AI agent overall, that encompasses both of these things. So essentially an AI agent consists of the AI model and the agentic harness. That's the tools and model uses. The way it remembers things, the loop that it keeps running, the rules about what it's allowed to do. All of that stuff lives inside the agentic harness. So let's get inside that harness. And what's inside is essentially three components. We've got tools. We've got memory and we've got the agentic loop. So let's take a look at these one at a time. We'll start with tools. So through tools, the model can do things out in the world. For example, one of the things it can do is it has access to files so it can read and write to them. Another thing we can do with tools is run code. And that code might run in a sandbox as well. We can go and get information on the internet. And we can also often actually drive a computer screen itself. This is called computer use. And here the model can move a cursor around and operate any software similar to the way that a person would do it. Now many of these capabilities are actually built into the harness directly. But anything else already on the machine, well, a harness usually gives the model access to the command line. So it can just run whatever software is already installed, which is really the same way that a developer would do it. And then for connecting to external services that don't live on the machine, so maybe a corporate database or a third party app, as a standard called MCP model context protocol. The tool built for MCP can plug into any harness that supports it without being rebuilt each time. So that's tools. What about memory? Well, models have a fixed context window, which is basically their working memory and once the conversation ends, that working memory is wiped clean. But the harness can help persist things. For example, it can persist instruction files. So things like an agents.md file, which sits in a project folder and gets loaded into the model's context at the start of every session. How the model knows the co-bases, conventions, or what libraries to use. Now within a session, when the context window starts filling up, the harness runs another process where it compacts that context window. So it summarizes what happened earlier. So the important parts stay around, but stuff like redundant tool outputs, all that stuff kind of gets pruned out. And then rather than dumping an entire code base into the model's context all out once the harness lets the model perform a search. So we can search the project sometimes with grep-like text search, sometimes with semantic search or code indexes, and then just kind of pull in only the pieces it needs. That's memory. And then there is the agentic loop. Now this is where the harness and the model work together to achieve a goal. So the model decides on a next step to achieve that goal. That's the plan stage. And then the harness takes that plan and actually performs an action on it. And that action is performed. We get some results. The model observes those results. And then the loop repeats around and around, sometimes just for a few seconds, sometimes for hours. And in addition to this cycle, modern harnesses run verification continuously all the way through the loop. The model runs test as it goes, maybe it takes screenshots of what it's built. And sometimes even spins up a separate model to act as a reviewer. So verification is pretty cool running these tests and checking the outputs and taking a peek at screenshots. And a model that double checks itself might run a lot longer without going off the rails. So that's tools, memory, and the agentic loop. Once the harness has all three of these running together, the kinds of things AI can actually do start looking very different from anything an AI model can do on its own. So I think we should also ask, why should we care about this distinction? AI model and agentic harness? Well, because once we can see the model and the harness as separate things, I think a lot of what's been going on in AI starts to make a bit more sense. Because most of the capability gains we've seen lately, they've come actually from the harness getting better. So which I mean better tools and memory handling and smarter agentic loops with verification. And of course with every new version, the models have improved as well. So when somebody asks, is AI good at something? Like is AI good at writing code or is AI good as a customer support chatbot? I think the more useful version of that question is to better define what we mean by AI. And specifically, we mean two things. We mean which AI model are we going to use in this scenario? But also if this is an agent, we need to ask which harness are we going to use with that AI model as well. Because the model can be brilliant in one harness and get stuck in another. And the line between these two things is also a bit fluid because capabilities that use to live entirely in the harness, like long horizon planning or self verification, they're starting to be trained directly into the models and things that used to be model behavior like consistency over a long task are increasingly shaped by harness conventions and project files, which brings us back to that brain in a jar. The brain itself, the AI model, continues to get smarter. There's no doubt about that. But you know what, it's not just the model getting smarter. It's not just the brain. It's also the jar, the agent, it harness.

### **Final Professional Meeting Summary**

#### **Key Concepts: AI Models vs. Agentic Harnesses**
- **AI Model (the "brain")**
  - The foundational neural network that processes inputs and generates responses.
  - Limited in functionality without external interaction (e.g., cannot access files, run code, or browse the web).
  - Performance benchmarks are now closely matched across models, making harness capabilities the primary differentiator.

- **Agentic Harness (the "body")**
  - A wrapper around the AI model that enables real-world interaction by providing:
    - **Tools**: File access, code execution, web browsing, computer use, command-line access, and external service integration (via MCP).
    - **Memory**: Retains and manages context (e.g., `agents.md` files) by compacting, pruning, and searching relevant information (text, semantic, or code-based).
    - **Agentic Loop**: A feedback-driven process where the model plans actions, the harness executes them, and the model observes results for continuous improvement and verification.

#### **MCP (Model Context Protocol)**
- A framework that enhances AI models by integrating tools, memory, and agentic loops through a harness.
- Enables seamless integration of third-party tools without rebuilding, allowing flexible and scalable functionality.

#### **Memory Management in AI Harnesses**
- **Context Window Limitations**: AI models have constrained working memory, requiring external systems to persist and manage critical information.
- **Compaction & Pruning**: The harness retains key details while removing redundancy to optimize performance.
- **Search & Retrieval**: Uses targeted search (text, semantic, or code-based) to pull only relevant parts of a codebase or dataset, improving efficiency.

#### **Agentic Loop & Verification**
- **Decision-Making Process**: The model plans steps, the harness executes actions, and the model observes outcomes in a continuous loop.
- **Continuous Verification**: Incorporates checks (tests, screenshots, peer reviews) to ensure reliability and prevent errors.
- **Task Duration & Consistency**: Extends task execution without derailing, with harness conventions and project files playing a growing role in maintaining consistency.

#### **Why the Harness Matters**
- The **harness** (not just the model) drives capability gains, including better tools, memory management, and agentic workflows.
- AI’s effectiveness depends on the synergy between the model and the harness, explaining recent advancements in AI performance.

#### **Key Takeaways**
- AI models alone are limited; harnesses unlock advanced functionality by managing tools, memory, and agentic workflows.
- The dynamic between the AI model (brain) and the harness (jar) is evolving, with both components improving in tandem.
- Future AI advancements will likely stem from innovations in harness design, verification processes, and tool integration.

#### **Action Items / Next Steps**
- Explore MCP (Model Context Protocol) for integrating third-party tools into AI workflows.
- Invest in harness development to enhance memory management, tool integration, and agentic loops.
- Focus on continuous verification and feedback mechanisms to improve AI reliability and task consistency.
